newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major and Blair both talk tough on Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major and Blair both talk tough on Europe.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Monday defiantly reaffirmed his determination to block an overhaul of European Union institutions unless Britain's partners agree to reform the bloc's fishing policies.

Major, facing deep splits in his Conservative party over Europe, was taking a firmer line on ties with the EU as he brought his campaign for the May 1 election to the fishing port of Newlyn in southwest England.

Not to be outdone, opposition leader Tony Blair said his Labour party was also prepared to wield Britain's veto unless it won policy changes to help the country's fishermen. Labour is favourite to win the election.
Blair's comments, which reflected his efforts to move the party into the centre of Britain's political spectrum, further blurred the dividing line between the two parties.

"Let me make one thing absolutely clear to you," he told a BBC radio interviewer. "Where Britain's interests are at stake, we are perfectly prepared to be isolated. What we don't seek is a policy of perpetual isolation."
Labour kicked off the week's electioneering by outlining its plans to improve the state education system and promised a more positive campaign.

Blair declared education an "economic imperative" and repeated pledges to make it the number one priority of his government, with the minister in charge ranking alongside the Chancellor of the Exchequer, or finance minister.
Party officials deny Labour's new emphasis on a positive message signals that Conservative attacks on Blair last week have hit home, denting Labour's huge opinion poll lead.

Major, speaking as EU fisheries ministers met in Luxembourg to discuss plans for further deep cuts in fishing quotas, said he was prepared to veto the EU's long-running inter-governmental conference (IGC) when it concludes in Amsterdam in June.

He earlier met fishermen angered by the EU's Common Fisheries Policy, which they say has encouraged foreign fishermen -- or "quota-hoppers" -- to grab an unfair share of declining British stocks by buying up British boats.
"The IGC won't come to a successful conclusion until... the problem of quota-hopping is resolved satisfactorily," said Major. "It cannot come to a solution without unanimity."
Major warned last year that he would block the IGC, crucial to EU's plans to expand from 15 members to more than 20 in the coming decade, if it did not solve the quota-hopping problem.

But doubts about the government's resolve were raised when the Conservative Research Department, according to Monday's Guardian newspaper, reprimanded Defence Secretary Michael Portillo for saying the government was prepared to veto the IGC.
Major sided firmly with Portillo. "I happen to be prime minister, not the Conservative Research Department," he said.

Conservatives splits over Europe have dogged Major's 6-1/2 years as prime minister, but he was happy to go on the offensive on Monday, accusing the Labour and minority Liberal Democrat parties of being ready to sell out Britain to Brussels.
But down on the quay in Newlyn, fishermen were sceptical that Major -- or for that matter Blair -- could turn a tide they fear will capsize their industry.
